claims.text: The catalytic performance of PGM-based nanoscale ethanol-oxidation catalysts is governed by dynamic surface-oxide coverage.
Surface oxide species modulate the binding and conversion of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
A partially oxidized PGM surface is typical after activation under standard ethanol-oxidation conditions.
A controlled passivation treatment can increase surface-oxide coverage without changing overall catalyst composition or morphology.
Local oxide coverage can be tracked through oxide-related vibrational features such as Pt-OH modes.
The appearance and disappearance of vibrational peaks from adsorbed organic intermediates report changes associated with local oxide coverage.
Moderate surface-oxide coverage stabilizes critical partially oxidized ethanol fragments.
Moderate surface-oxide coverage facilitates efficient electron and proton transfer and thereby promotes complete ethanol oxidation.
Oxide coverage above an optimal threshold overly stabilizes or traps reaction intermediates.
Excessive oxide coverage reduces turnover and alters product selectivity.
Under baseline conditions, an optimal intensity of Pt-OH and intermediate-specific vibrational peaks will correlate with high current density and selective complete oxidation to CO2.
Passivation will produce stronger oxide-related vibrational signals and altered intermediate peak intensities.
Passivation-induced increases in oxide coverage will reduce turnover and shift selectivity toward partial oxidation products.
The proposed oxide-coverage relationship applies at potentials and electrolyte conditions that promote multi-electron ethanol oxidation.
The correlation between oxide coverage and catalytic performance may break down on a highly reduced surface or under non-oxidative conditions.
